# Canvas, layers, text and shapes

The preview canvas is where you place a clip's picture. Select a layer on it,
then drag to move, scale, rotate or crop it. The Clip tab's **Picture**
sub-tab holds the same placement as numbers, along with opacity, blend modes,
shadows, filters and the effects that hide or highlight part of a frame. This
page also covers what you can put on the canvas besides footage: text clips,
shape clips, image clips, background plates, and matte tracks, which cut the
track behind them.

Every clip that draws can be edited the same way: video, image, still, text,
shape, graphic and nest. A track never holds just one kind of clip. Tracks
stack back to front, and a track higher in the timeline draws in front.

## The canvas

The canvas shows the composition at the playhead, at the project's size,
centred in the preview pane. Under it is a small caption with the canvas size
and frame rate, for example `1920 × 1080 · 30 fps`. You set the canvas size,
rate and background colour on the Document tab (see
[Projects and media](projects-and-media.md)).

### Zoom and pan

| Do this | To |
|---|---|
| Toolbar zoom popup: **Fit**, **50%**, **100%**, **200%** | Pick a zoom stop |
| **View ▸ Zoom In** (⌘+ or ⌘=), **View ▸ Zoom Out** (⌘-) | Step through the same four stops |
| **View ▸ Zoom to Fit** (⌘0) | Go back to Fit |
| Pinch on the trackpad, or ⌥-scroll / ⌘-scroll | Step through the stops |
| Hold Space and drag, or scroll | Pan, when the zoomed canvas is bigger than the pane |

A Space tap that does not pan still plays and pauses as usual.

**View ▸ Preview Window** (⇧⌘P) opens a second window with the same picture
and no handles, for a second display.

### Selecting

- Click a layer to select the topmost visible clip under the pointer at the
  playhead. Hit-testing follows the layer's rotation.
- ⇧-click adds a clip to the selection or removes it.
- Click empty canvas to clear the selection.
- Clips on hidden tracks are not drawn, so you can't click them. Clips on
  locked tracks are drawn but can't be selected or moved on the canvas.
- A clip on a matte track can be selected and dragged like any other clip
  inside its own box, even though it draws nothing there (see
  [Matte tracks](#matte-tracks)). Because it is topmost inside that box, a
  click there selects the matte clip. To select the clip it cuts, click
  outside the matte clip's box, or use the timeline.

The selected clips get an outline. The front-most selected clip also gets
handles.

### Move, scale and rotate

| Gesture | What it does |
|---|---|
| Drag inside the box | Move. Every selected clip moves by the same amount |
| ← → ↑ ↓ (canvas focused) | Nudge the selection 1 canvas pixel |
| ⇧ + arrow | Nudge 10 pixels |
| Drag one of the eight square handles | Scale (see below) |
| ⌥ while scaling | Scale about the centre instead of pinning the opposite handle |
| Drag the round grip above the top edge | Rotate about the clip's centre |
| ⇧ while rotating | Snap the angle to 15° steps |
| Esc during any drag | Cancel the drag and put the clip back where it was, with no undo step |

How a scale drag behaves depends on the clip:

- **Video, image, still, graphic and nest clips** have one uniform scale. Every
  handle scales the whole picture and keeps its aspect ratio.
- **Shape clips** change their box size instead. A corner handle keeps the
  aspect ratio and ⇧ frees it. An edge handle changes only the width or only
  the height.
- **Text clips**: the left and right edge handles set the text box's wrap
  width, which makes the box fixed-width. The corners and the top and bottom
  edges scale the text uniformly.

A drag scales between 1 % and 1000 %. Each drag is one undo step, and a click
that doesn't move anything adds no step.

There is no separate anchor-point control. Rotation, the Picture tab's Scale
field and a ⌥ scale drag pivot on the centre of the clip's uncropped picture.
A plain handle drag keeps the opposite handle in place by moving the clip as
it scales.

### Line and arrow endpoints

A line or arrow shape has a round handle at each end. Drag a handle to move
that end. The scale handles and the rotation grip still work on the line's
box.

### Snapping

While you drag a clip to move it, the box snaps to:

- the canvas edges, its centre lines and its thirds
- the edges and centres of every other visible layer

Scaling, rotating and cropping do not snap (⇧ while rotating snaps the angle
to 15° steps instead). A guide line is drawn across the canvas on each axis that snapped. Press
**N** or choose **View ▸ Snapping** to turn snapping on or off. The timeline
uses the same setting. Hold ⌘ during a drag to stop snapping for that drag.

### Safe areas

**View ▸ Safe Areas**, or the toolbar's **Safe** checkbox, draws two guide
frames over the canvas, at 90 % and 80 % of its size. They are guides only
and never appear in an export. The app remembers the setting.

### Editing an action's end state on the canvas

With an action selected on the clip's action lane, a move, scale, rotate or
crop drag, or an arrow-key nudge, edits that action's end state, just as the
inspector's fields do. The box on screen still shows the frame at the
playhead. There are two exceptions: a drag on a multi-clip selection, and a
shape's box resize, both edit the clip itself. See
[Motion and transitions](motion-and-transitions.md).

## Crop

Press **C**, or double-click a clip that is not text, to enter crop mode for
the selected clip. The eight handles become crop edges, and the part being
cut away is shown as a dim ghost inside the uncropped frame. Press **Esc** or
**Return**, or click empty canvas, to leave crop mode.

A crop removes edges in place: the picture never shifts as you crop. Crop
amounts are in the source's own pixels, so they stay correct when you scale
the clip later. The core keeps at least one source pixel in each direction.

The Picture tab's **Crop** section has the same four insets as fields, plus a
**Crop on Canvas** button that enters crop mode. Crop appears only for clips
with pixels of their own, which means video, image and still clips.

## Inline text editing

Double-click a text clip on the canvas to type into it in place. The editor
uses the clip's own font, tracking and line spacing at the canvas's zoom, and
it grows and wraps as you type, the way the text will once you apply it.
UPPERCASE text is edited as you typed it.

STUB
set_selection Selects clips — clicking one in the timeline or on the canvas, and Edit ▸ Select All (⌘A). View state like the playhead and the range: nothing is undoable and the project is untouched. It matters because the canvas handles, crop mode and every inspector pane act on the SELECTION, so this is how you put the app into the state a screenshot should show. Call it with no clips (or []) to select nothing; get_project reports the result as selection. Note that the ops themselves take their own clips argument — selecting is not a prerequisite for editing.
set_video Changes the clips' BASE video properties — position, scale, rotation, opacity, crop, corner radius, shadow, colour, chroma key, filters, reflection, spotlight and motion (what the clip does on its way in, on its way out and all the way through). The patch MERGES AT EVERY DEPTH: keys you leave out keep their values, inside a nested object too — a patch of just {shadow: {blur: 20}} keeps the shadow's colour, angle and distance — and shadow, chroma, reflection, spotlight or motion set to null clears it. A LIST is the exception: filters and obscure each replace whole, so send the whole stack and [
render_frame Renders one frame of the finished timeline as a picture so you can SEE the result — the verification hook. It goes through the same composition and the same Metal compositor an export does, so this is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it. The image comes back both as an image block and as a file on disk whose path the text names. Use it before and after every edit. It writes a PNG to a temporary file unless path or format says otherwise, so a call that names neither is exactly the call it always was. # CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, Node is pinned by `.node-version`. `README.md` has the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

</system-reminder>

---
title: "The canvas"
description: "What the preview's canvas shows, how clips stack on it, and what you can do directly on the picture."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

The canvas is the fixed frame every clip is drawn into. It's where you place a clip's picture, and every export starts from it.

<AtAGlance
  where={['The preview pane', 'Document tab, for its size, rate and background']}
  tools={['render_frame', 'set_video', 'set_selection']}
/>

<Shot
  name="04-editor.window"
  alt="The editor with nothing selected. In the preview pane a black 960 × 540 canvas sits in a grey surround, showing a navy video clip smaller than the frame, the words Frame Job inside a white ellipse in front of it, and a lower-third title at the bottom left. The caption under the picture reads 960 × 540 · 30 fps."
/>

## What the canvas shows

The canvas shows the composition at the playhead, at the project's size, centred in the preview pane with a margin of 24 points round it. A thin line marks its edge, so a black canvas still shows against the dark surround.

A clip smaller than the canvas leaves the background colour showing around it. A clip larger than the canvas is cut off at its edge.

You don't set the canvas up here. Its size is on [Canvas size](/projects/canvas-size/), and its rate and background colour are on the [Document tab](/projects/document-tab/).

## The caption

The small line under the picture states the canvas size and frame rate, for example `1920 × 1080 · 30 fps`.

## Layers

Tracks stack back to front, so a track higher in the timeline draws in front of the ones below it. A track doesn't hold one kind of clip: video, image, still, text, shape, graphic and nest clips can share a track, and you place them all with the same gestures and the same Picture sections, apart from the exceptions on their own pages.

An adjustment clip has no picture of its own, so it has no box on the canvas. Select it on the timeline. See [Adjustment clips](/color/adjustment-clips/).

## Working on the canvas

Drag on the picture and the placement changes. The [Picture tab](/canvas/picture-tab/) shows the same placement as numbers.

| To | Do this | More |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Select a clip | Click it. | [Select on the canvas](/canvas/select-on-canvas/) |
| Move a clip | Drag inside its box, or press an arrow key. | [Move](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#move) |
| Resize a clip | Drag one of the eight square handles. | [Scale](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#scale) |
| Rotate a clip | Drag the round grip above the top edge. | [Rotate](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#rotate) |
| Crop a clip | Press <kbd>C</kbd>, or double-click a clip that isn't text. | [Crop](/canvas/crop/) |
| Change a title's words | Double-click a text clip. | [Edit text on the canvas](/text-and-shapes/edit-text-on-canvas/) |
| Move one end of a line or arrow | Drag its round end handle. | [Lines and arrows](/text-and-shapes/lines-and-arrows/) |

Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> during a drag to [cancel it](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#cancel-a-drag).

### With an action selected

While an action is selected on the clip, a move, scale, rotate or crop drag and an arrow-key nudge change that action's end state, as the inspector's fields do. The box on screen still shows the frame at the playhead. See [Select an action](/motion/select-an-action/).

Two things always change the clip itself: resizing a shape's box and dragging a line's end. Several clips selected at once have no selected action, so a drag on them changes the clips too.

## Hidden and locked tracks

Clips on a hidden track aren't drawn, so you can't click them. A clip with its [picture turned off](/editing/enable-picture-and-sound/) draws nothing either, and can't be clicked.

Clips on a [locked track](/timeline/hide-and-lock-tracks/) are drawn, but you can't select or move them on the canvas. A click passes through to whatever is behind.

- A locked clip you select on the timeline shows its outline on the canvas, with no handles.
- If the front-most selected clip is locked, nothing gets handles, even when an unlocked clip is selected behind it.
- A drag or an arrow-key nudge of several clips leaves any on a locked track where they are.

## Canvas modes

Some tools wait for a click or a drag on the picture. While one is armed the pointer is a crosshair, a hint pill at the top of the canvas says what to do, and the canvas takes every press.

| Mode | Arm it with | The hint reads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Zoom to Region](/motion/zoom-to-region/) | <kbd>Z</kbd>, or the Zoom to Region button above the action lane | "Drag a rectangle to zoom to it · ⇧ fills · Esc to cancel" |
| [Place on Canvas](/effects/obscure/) | **Place on Canvas** in the Obscure section | "Drag a rectangle to obscure · Esc to cancel" |
| [Pick from Canvas](/effects/chroma-key/), for a chroma key | **Pick from Canvas** in the Chroma Key section | "Click to pick the key color · Esc to cancel" |
| [Pick from Canvas](/color/pick-from-canvas/), for a qualifier | **Pick from Canvas** in the Qualifier section | "Click to pick the colour to qualify · Esc to cancel" |

Only one mode can be armed at a time, and arming one ends the other. A mode ends when:

- you finish the drag or the pick
- you press <kbd>Esc</kbd>, which changes nothing
- you press its key or button a second time
- the selection changes so that it's no longer aimed at the same clips

Zoom to Region and Place on Canvas need exactly one selected clip that's drawing at the playhead and isn't on a locked track. Otherwise Frame Job beeps and the mode doesn't start. The two pick modes beep the same way when nothing selected can use them.

## With an agent

`render_frame` writes the frame at a moment as a picture file, through the same path an export takes, so an agent can look at what it made. See [Check the picture: render_frame](/mcp/render-frame/).

## Related

- [Zoom and pan the preview](/canvas/zoom-and-pan/)
- [Canvas snapping](/canvas/canvas-snapping/)
- [Safe areas](/canvas/safe-areas/)
- [Matte tracks](/canvas/matte-tracks/)

---
title: "Zoom and pan the preview"
description: "Look closer at the picture with the zoom popup, the View menu or a pinch, and move around a canvas bigger than the pane."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Zoom the preview to look closely at the picture or to place something precisely, then pan to reach the part you want. Zooming is only a way of looking: it changes nothing in the project, makes no undo step and is never exported.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['View ▸ Zoom In', 'View ▸ Zoom Out', 'View ▸ Zoom to Fit']}
  keys={['⌘+', '⌘=', '⌘-', '⌘0']}
  where={['The zoom popup in the toolbar', 'Pinch, ⌥-scroll or ⌘-scroll over the preview', 'Scroll or Space-drag to pan']}
/>

## The zoom popup

The popup in the toolbar sets how large the picture appears. Its stops are **Fit**, **50%**, **100%** and **200%**. It always shows the zoom the canvas is at, however you got there.

**Fit** sizes the canvas to the pane and follows the pane as it changes. At **100%**, one canvas pixel takes one point on screen.

Each window starts at **Fit**, and the zoom isn't saved with the project.

## View menu commands

| Command | Key | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **View ▸ Zoom In** | <kbd>⌘+</kbd> or <kbd>⌘=</kbd> | Goes to the next stop up. Greyed at 200%. |
| **View ▸ Zoom Out** | <kbd>⌘-</kbd> | Goes to the next stop down. Greyed at Fit. |
| **View ▸ Zoom to Fit** | <kbd>⌘0</kbd> | Goes straight back to Fit and centres the canvas. Greyed at Fit. |

These zoom the preview. To zoom the timeline, see [Zoom and scroll the timeline](/timeline/zoom-and-scroll/).

## Pinch and scroll

Pinch on a trackpad over the preview, or scroll with <kbd>⌥</kbd> or <kbd>⌘</kbd> held, to step through the same four stops. The stops are separate steps, so a gesture has to build up a little before it takes the next one.

## Panning

When the zoomed canvas is bigger than the pane, there are two ways to move it:

- Scroll over the preview.
- Hold <kbd>Space</kbd> and drag. Click the canvas first if it doesn't have focus, because the canvas has to be holding the keyboard for <kbd>Space</kbd> to reach it.

A pan only works along a side where the canvas overflows the pane, so you can't drag the canvas out of view. While the canvas fits, a plain scroll does nothing.

Moving between stops keeps your pan, pulled back if it no longer fits. Going back to **Fit** centres the canvas again.

## Space on the canvas

With the canvas focused, <kbd>Space</kbd> still plays and pauses. Frame Job can't tell a tap from a pan until you let go, so playback starts or stops on the release rather than the press. If you panned while <kbd>Space</kbd> was down, the release does nothing to playback.

## Good to know

- The stops count up from **Fit** in order, whatever size Fit happens to be. On a small canvas in a large pane, **50%** can be smaller than **Fit**.
- While the canvas fits, holding <kbd>Space</kbd> and dragging a clip moves the clip as usual, and playback toggles when you let go of <kbd>Space</kbd>.

## Related

- [The canvas](/canvas/the-canvas/)
- [Preview Quality](/timeline/preview-quality/)
- [The Preview Window](/timeline/preview-window/)
- [Play, pause and shuttle](/timeline/playback/)

---
title: "Select on the canvas"
description: "Pick clips by clicking them in the preview, add to or clear the selection, and read the frame and handles a selected clip gets."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

Click a clip in the preview to work on it there, without hunting for it on the timeline. It's the same selection the timeline and the inspector use.

<AtAGlance keys="⇧-click" where="The preview canvas" tools="set_selection" />

<Shot
  name="05-clip-picture.window"
  alt="A video clip selected in the editor. In the preview it has a thin coral outline with white square handles at its four corners and the middle of its four edges, and a round grip on a short stalk above its top edge. The inspector's Clip tab shows the clip's Picture sub-tab."
/>

## Click a layer

Click the picture to select the front-most visible clip under the pointer at the playhead. The test follows the layer's rotation, so a turned clip is selected by the shape you can see, not by the box it would have upright.

The selected clip's handles come first: a handle lying on top of another clip still grabs the handle, so you can resize a clip that has others in front of it.

Clicking a clip that's already part of a multiple selection keeps the whole selection, so you can drag them together. To narrow it down to one clip, click empty canvas first or use the [timeline](/timeline/selecting-clips/).

## Shift-click

<kbd>⇧</kbd>-click adds a clip to the selection, or takes it out if it's already selected.

## Click the void

Click empty canvas, or the dark area around it, to clear the selection. This also leaves [crop mode](/canvas/crop/).

With <kbd>⇧</kbd> held the selection stays, and crop mode still ends.

## The selection frame

Every selected clip that's drawing at the playhead gets a coral outline with a dark backing line, so it shows on both light and dark pictures. The front-most selected clip has a heavier outline and carries the handles:

- Eight white square handles, at the corners and the middle of each edge, for [scaling](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#scale).
- A round grip on a stalk above the top edge, for [rotating](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#rotate).
- On a [line or arrow](/text-and-shapes/lines-and-arrows/), a round handle at each end as well.

The handles stay the same size on screen at every zoom. The pointer shows what a handle does: a left-right or up-down resize pointer on an edge handle, and a crosshair on a corner.

A selected clip that isn't at the playhead has no frame, because it isn't in the picture. An adjustment clip never has one, because it has no rectangle of its own.

## Matte clips

A clip on a [matte track](/canvas/matte-tracks/) can be selected and dragged inside its own box, even though it draws nothing there.

Because it's the front-most clip inside that box, a click there selects the matte clip. To select the clip it cuts, click outside the matte clip's box, or use the timeline.

## Good to know

Clips on hidden tracks can't be clicked, and clips on locked tracks are passed over. See [Hidden and locked tracks](/canvas/the-canvas/#hidden-and-locked-tracks).

## Related

- [Move, scale and rotate](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/)
- [Select clips](/timeline/selecting-clips/)
- [Crop](/canvas/crop/)
- [Edit text on the canvas](/text-and-shapes/edit-text-on-canvas/)

---
title: "Move, scale and rotate"
description: "Place a clip directly on the picture with drags, arrow keys, the eight handles and the rotation grip."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Select a clip on the canvas, then drag it into place. The handles and the grip do the same job as the numbers on the [Picture tab](/canvas/transform/), with the picture in front of you.

<AtAGlance
  keys={['← → ↑ ↓', '⇧ + arrow', '⌥-drag', '⇧-drag', 'Esc']}
  where="The preview canvas"
  tools="set_video"
/>

## Move

Drag inside a clip's box to move it. Every selected clip moves by the same amount and keeps its place relative to the others, including a selected clip that isn't at the playhead. Clips on locked tracks stay where they are.

The move [snaps](/canvas/canvas-snapping/) to the canvas and to other layers. Snapping tests the clip you grabbed, so the whole selection clicks into place together.

## Nudge

With the canvas focused, the arrow keys move the selected clips one canvas pixel. Hold <kbd>⇧</kbd> to move them ten. Clicking the canvas gives it focus.

Each press is one undo step, called Nudge. A nudge doesn't snap, and clips on locked tracks stay put.

With nothing selected, or only locked clips, the keys do their usual job: <kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd> step the playhead by a frame, <kbd>⇧←</kbd> and <kbd>⇧→</kbd> by ten, and <kbd>↑</kbd> and <kbd>↓</kbd> go to the previous and next edit point.

## Scale

Drag a corner or edge handle. The opposite handle stays pinned in place, and the clip moves as it scales to keep it there. This works on a rotated clip too.

What a handle changes depends on the clip:

| Clip | Corner handles | Edge handles |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Video, image, still, graphic, nest | Scale the whole picture and keep its shape. | The same. A clip like this has one scale, so an edge handle can't stretch it. |
| [Shape](/text-and-shapes/shape-settings/) | Resize the box and keep its proportions. Hold <kbd>⇧</kbd> to free them. | Change only the width or only the height. |
| [Text](/text-and-shapes/text-box/) | Scale the text. | Left and right set the wrap width, with the clip's centre staying still. Top and bottom scale the text. |

A drag scales between 1 % and 1000 %. A shape's box and a text clip's wrap width stay between 4 and 20,000.

A drag acts on the front-most selected clip only, even with several selected.

## Scale about the centre

Hold <kbd>⌥</kbd> while you scale to keep the clip's centre still instead of the opposite handle.

## Rotate

Drag the round grip above the top edge to turn the clip about its centre. A positive angle turns it clockwise. However far you drag, the angle stays between −180° and 180°, so the inspector never shows a wound-up value.

## Snap the angle

Hold <kbd>⇧</kbd> while you rotate to snap the angle to 15° steps.

## Cancel a drag

Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> during a canvas drag to put everything back as it was at the press, with no undo step. This covers move, scale, rotate, crop, line end and obscure region drags. Timeline drags have no such cancel.

<kbd>⇧</kbd> can stay down, but <kbd>Esc</kbd> doesn't cancel while <kbd>⌥</kbd> or <kbd>⌘</kbd> is held, so let go of those first.

## The pivot

Rotation, the Picture tab's **Scale** field and a <kbd>⌥</kbd> scale drag all pivot on the centre of the clip's uncropped picture. There's no separate anchor-point control. Because the pivot is the uncropped centre, cropping never moves it.

## One undo step per drag

Each canvas drag is one undo step, however many clips it moved, and a click that moves nothing adds no step. The steps are named Move, Scale, Rotate and Crop, so the Edit menu reads **Undo Move**, for example.

## Good to know

- With an action selected, these gestures change that action's end state rather than the clip. See [With an action selected](/canvas/the-canvas/#with-an-action-selected).
- In [crop mode](/canvas/crop/) the eight handles crop the clip instead of scaling it.

## Related

- [Position, scale, rotation and opacity](/canvas/transform/)
- [Canvas snapping](/canvas/canvas-snapping/)
- [Lines and arrows](/text-and-shapes/lines-and-arrows/)
- [Undo and saving](/getting-started/undo-and-saving/)

---
title: "Canvas snapping"
description: "Line a clip up with the canvas and other layers as you move it, and turn the pull off for one drag."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

While you move a clip on the canvas, its box pulls into line with the canvas and with the other layers, and a guide line shows what it lined up with.

<AtAGlance
  menu="View ▸ Snapping"
  keys={['N', '⌘-drag']}
  where="The Snap checkbox in the timeline bar"
/>

## What snaps

Only a move snaps. While you drag a clip, its box snaps to:

- the canvas's edges, its centre lines and its thirds
- the edges and centres of every other layer drawn at the playhead, including clips on locked tracks

Frame Job tests the clip's edges and its centre on each axis, and the smallest correction wins. The pull reaches 8 points on screen at any zoom, so it covers fewer canvas pixels the further you zoom in. A snap always lands on a whole canvas pixel.

A turned clip snaps by the bounds of its rotated box. With several clips selected, the clip you grabbed is the one tested, and the others in the drag aren't targets.

Scaling, rotating, cropping and arrow-key nudges don't snap. <kbd>⇧</kbd> while rotating [snaps the angle](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#snap-the-angle) instead.

## Guide lines

A guide line is drawn across the whole canvas on each axis that snapped, so you can see what the clip lined up with. It's only there during the drag.

## Suspend for one drag

Hold <kbd>⌘</kbd> during a drag to stop snapping for as long as it's down. It works from the press or at any point during the drag, and snapping comes back when you let go of <kbd>⌘</kbd>.

## Turn snapping off

Press <kbd>N</kbd>, choose **View ▸ Snapping**, or use the **Snap** checkbox in the timeline bar. Snapping is on to begin with, and Frame Job remembers your choice. The canvas and the timeline share the one setting. See [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/).

## Related

- [Move, scale and rotate](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/)
- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
- [Safe areas](/canvas/safe-areas/)

---
title: "Safe areas"
description: "Show guide frames over the picture to keep titles and action clear of the canvas's edges."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Safe areas are two guide frames over the picture. Use them to keep titles and important action away from the edges, where a screen or a player's controls can cover them.

<AtAGlance
  menu="View ▸ Safe Areas"
  where="The Safe checkbox in the toolbar"
/>

## Safe area guides

Choose **View ▸ Safe Areas**, or tick **Safe** in the toolbar. Two centred frames appear, one at 90 % of the canvas's width and height and one at 80 %. On a 1920 × 1080 canvas that's 1728 × 972 and 1536 × 864.

The frames aren't labelled, and the inner one is drawn fainter. The menu item has a checkmark while they show.

The guides are off to begin with, and Frame Job remembers your choice between launches.

## Good to know

- The percentages are of the canvas, not the pane, so the frames zoom and pan with the picture.
- They take no clicks, so everything under them still works.
- They're guides only. They never appear in an export or a saved frame.

## Related

- [The canvas](/canvas/the-canvas/)
- [Canvas size](/projects/canvas-size/)
- [Canvas snapping](/canvas/canvas-snapping/)

---
title: "The canvas"
description: "What the preview's canvas shows, how clips stack on it, and what you can do directly on the picture."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

The canvas is the fixed frame every clip is drawn into. It's where you place a clip's picture, and every export starts from it.

<AtAGlance
  where={['The preview pane', 'Document tab, for its size, rate and background']}
  tools={['render_frame', 'set_video', 'set_selection']}
/>

<Shot
  name="04-editor.window"
  alt="The editor with nothing selected. In the preview pane a black 960 × 540 canvas sits in a grey surround, showing a navy video clip smaller than the frame, the words Frame Job inside a white ellipse in front of it, and a lower-third title at the bottom left. The caption under the picture reads 960 × 540 · 30 fps."
/>

## What the canvas shows

The canvas shows the composition at the playhead, at the project's size, centred in the preview pane with a margin of 24 points round it. A thin line marks its edge, so a black canvas still shows against the dark surround.

A clip smaller than the canvas leaves the background colour showing around it. A clip larger than the canvas is cut off at its edge.

You don't set the canvas up here. Its size is on [Canvas size](/projects/canvas-size/), and its rate and background colour are on the [Document tab](/projects/document-tab/).

## The caption

The small line under the picture states the canvas size and frame rate, for example `1920 × 1080 · 30 fps`.

## Layers

Tracks stack back to front, so a track higher in the timeline draws in front of the ones below it. A track doesn't hold one kind of clip: video, image, still, text, shape, graphic and nest clips can share a track, and you place them all with the same gestures and the same Picture sections, apart from the exceptions on their own pages.

An adjustment clip has no picture of its own, so it has no box on the canvas. Select it on the timeline. See [Adjustment clips](/color/adjustment-clips/).

## Working on the canvas

Drag on the picture and the placement changes. The [Picture tab](/canvas/picture-tab/) shows the same placement as numbers.

| To | Do this | More |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Select a clip | Click it. | [Select on the canvas](/canvas/select-on-canvas/) |
| Move a clip | Drag inside its box, or press an arrow key. | [Move](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#move) |
| Resize a clip | Drag one of the eight square handles. | [Scale](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#scale) |
| Rotate a clip | Drag the round grip above the top edge. | [Rotate](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#rotate) |
| Crop a clip | Press <kbd>C</kbd>, or double-click a clip that isn't text. | [Crop](/canvas/crop/) |
| Change a title's words | Double-click a text clip. | [Edit text on the canvas](/text-and-shapes/edit-text-on-canvas/) |
| Move one end of a line or arrow | Drag its round end handle. | [Lines and arrows](/text-and-shapes/lines-and-arrows/) |

Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> during a drag to [cancel it](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#cancel-a-drag).

### With an action selected

While an action is selected on the clip, a move, scale, rotate or crop drag and an arrow-key nudge change that action's end state, as the inspector's fields do. The box on screen still shows the frame at the playhead. See [Select an action](/motion/select-an-action/).

Two things always change the clip itself: resizing a shape's box and dragging a line's end. Several clips selected at once have no selected action, so a drag on them changes the clips too.

## Hidden and locked tracks

Clips on a hidden track aren't drawn, so you can't click them. A clip with its [picture turned off](/editing/enable-picture-and-sound/) draws nothing either, and can't be clicked.

Clips on a [locked track](/timeline/hide-and-lock-tracks/) are drawn, but you can't select or move them on the canvas. A click passes through to whatever is behind.

- A locked clip you select on the timeline shows its outline on the canvas, with no handles.
- If the front-most selected clip is locked, nothing gets handles, even when an unlocked clip is selected behind it.
- A drag or an arrow-key nudge of several clips leaves any on a locked track where they are.

## Canvas modes

Some tools wait for a click or a drag on the picture. While one is armed the pointer is a crosshair, a hint pill at the top of the canvas says what to do, and the canvas takes every press.

| Mode | Arm it with | The hint reads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Zoom to Region](/motion/zoom-to-region/) | <kbd>Z</kbd>, or the Zoom to Region button above the action lane | "Drag a rectangle to zoom to it · ⇧ fills · Esc to cancel" |
| [Place on Canvas](/effects/obscure/) | **Place on Canvas** in the Obscure section | "Drag a rectangle to obscure · Esc to cancel" |
| [Pick from Canvas](/effects/chroma-key/), for a chroma key | **Pick from Canvas** in the Chroma Key section | "Click to pick the key color · Esc to cancel" |
| [Pick from Canvas](/color/pick-from-canvas/), for a qualifier | **Pick from Canvas** in the Qualifier section | "Click to pick the colour to qualify · Esc to cancel" |

Only one mode can be armed at a time, and arming one ends the other. A mode ends when:

- you finish the drag or the pick
- you press <kbd>Esc</kbd>, which changes nothing
- you press its key or button a second time
- the selection changes so that it's no longer aimed at the same clips

Zoom to Region and Place on Canvas need exactly one selected clip that's drawing at the playhead and isn't on a locked track. Otherwise Frame Job beeps and the mode doesn't start. The two pick modes beep the same way when nothing selected can use them.

## With an agent

`render_frame` writes the frame at a moment as a picture file, through the same path an export takes, so an agent can look at what it made. See [Check the picture: render_frame](/mcp/render-frame/).

## Related

- [Zoom and pan the preview](/canvas/zoom-and-pan/)
- [Canvas snapping](/canvas/canvas-snapping/)
- [Safe areas](/canvas/safe-areas/)
- [Matte tracks](/canvas/matte-tracks/)

---
title: "Zoom and pan the preview"
description: "Look closer at the picture with the zoom popup, the View menu or a pinch, and move around a canvas bigger than the pane."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Zoom the preview to look closely at the picture or to place something precisely, then pan to reach the part you want. Zooming is only a way of looking: it changes nothing in the project, makes no undo step and is never exported.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['View ▸ Zoom In', 'View ▸ Zoom Out', 'View ▸ Zoom to Fit']}
  keys={['⌘+', '⌘=', '⌘-', '⌘0']}
  where={['The zoom popup in the toolbar', 'Pinch, ⌥-scroll or ⌘-scroll over the preview', 'Scroll or Space-drag to pan']}
/>

## The zoom popup

The popup in the toolbar sets how large the picture appears. Its stops are **Fit**, **50%**, **100%** and **200%**. It always shows the zoom the canvas is at, however you got there.

**Fit** sizes the canvas to the pane and follows the pane as it changes. At **100%**, one canvas pixel takes one point on screen.

Each window starts at **Fit**, and the zoom isn't saved with the project.

## View menu commands

| Command | Key | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **View ▸ Zoom In** | <kbd>⌘+</kbd> or <kbd>⌘=</kbd> | Goes to the next stop up. Greyed at 200%. |
| **View ▸ Zoom Out** | <kbd>⌘-</kbd> | Goes to the next stop down. Greyed at Fit. |
| **View ▸ Zoom to Fit** | <kbd>⌘0</kbd> | Goes straight back to Fit and centres the canvas. Greyed at Fit. |

These zoom the preview. To zoom the timeline, see [Zoom and scroll the timeline](/timeline/zoom-and-scroll/).

## Pinch and scroll

Pinch on a trackpad over the preview, or scroll with <kbd>⌥</kbd> or <kbd>⌘</kbd> held, to step through the same four stops. The stops are separate steps, so a gesture has to build up a little before it takes the next one.

## Panning

When the zoomed canvas is bigger than the pane, there are two ways to move it:

- Scroll over the preview.
- Hold <kbd>Space</kbd> and drag. Click the canvas first if it doesn't have focus, because the canvas has to be holding the keyboard for <kbd>Space</kbd> to reach it.

A pan only works along a side where the canvas overflows the pane, so you can't drag the canvas out of view. While the canvas fits, a plain scroll does nothing.

Moving between stops keeps your pan, pulled back if it no longer fits. Going back to **Fit** centres the canvas again.

## Space on the canvas

With the canvas focused, <kbd>Space</kbd> still plays and pauses. Frame Job can't tell a tap from a pan until you let go, so playback starts or stops on the release rather than the press. If you panned while <kbd>Space</kbd> was down, the release does nothing to playback.

## Good to know

- The stops count up from **Fit** in order, whatever size Fit happens to be. On a small canvas in a large pane, **50%** can be smaller than **Fit**.
- While the canvas fits, holding <kbd>Space</kbd> and dragging a clip moves the clip as usual, and playback toggles when you let go of <kbd>Space</kbd>.

## Related

- [The canvas](/canvas/the-canvas/)
- [Preview Quality](/timeline/preview-quality/)
- [The Preview Window](/timeline/preview-window/)
- [Play, pause and shuttle](/timeline/playback/)

---
title: "Select on the canvas"
description: "Pick clips by clicking them in the preview, add to or clear the selection, and read the frame and handles a selected clip gets."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

Click a clip in the preview to work on it there, without hunting for it on the timeline. It's the same selection the timeline and the inspector use.

<AtAGlance keys="⇧-click" where="The preview canvas" tools="set_selection" />

<Shot
  name="05-clip-picture.window"
  alt="A video clip selected in the editor. In the preview it has a thin coral outline with white square handles at its four corners and the middle of its four edges, and a round grip on a short stalk above its top edge. The inspector's Clip tab shows the clip's Picture sub-tab."
/>

## Click a layer

Click the picture to select the front-most visible clip under the pointer at the playhead. The test follows the layer's rotation, so a turned clip is selected by the shape you can see, not by the box it would have upright.

The selected clip's handles come first: a handle lying on top of another clip still grabs the handle, so you can resize a clip that has others in front of it.

Clicking a clip that's already part of a multiple selection keeps the whole selection, so you can drag them together. To narrow it down to one clip, click empty canvas first or use the [timeline](/timeline/selecting-clips/).

## Shift-click

<kbd>⇧</kbd>-click adds a clip to the selection, or takes it out if it's already selected.

## Click the void

Click empty canvas, or the dark area around it, to clear the selection. This also leaves [crop mode](/canvas/crop/).

With <kbd>⇧</kbd> held the selection stays, and crop mode still ends.

## The selection frame

Every selected clip that's drawing at the playhead gets a coral outline with a dark backing line, so it shows on both light and dark pictures. The front-most selected clip has a heavier outline and carries the handles:

- Eight white square handles, at the corners and the middle of each edge, for [scaling](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#scale).
- A round grip on a stalk above the top edge, for [rotating](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#rotate).
- On a [line or arrow](/text-and-shapes/lines-and-arrows/), a round handle at each end as well.

The handles stay the same size on screen at every zoom. The pointer shows what a handle does: a left-right or up-down resize pointer on an edge handle, and a crosshair on a corner.

A selected clip that isn't at the playhead has no frame, because it isn't in the picture. An adjustment clip never has one, because it has no rectangle of its own.

## Matte clips

A clip on a [matte track](/canvas/matte-tracks/) can be selected and dragged inside its own box, even though it draws nothing there.

Because it's the front-most clip inside that box, a click there selects the matte clip. To select the clip it cuts, click outside the matte clip's box, or use the timeline.

## Good to know

Clips on hidden tracks can't be clicked, and clips on locked tracks are passed over. See [Hidden and locked tracks](/canvas/the-canvas/#hidden-and-locked-tracks).

## Related

- [Move, scale and rotate](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/)
- [Select clips](/timeline/selecting-clips/)
- [Crop](/canvas/crop/)
- [Edit text on the canvas](/text-and-shapes/edit-text-on-canvas/)

---
title: "Move, scale and rotate"
description: "Place a clip directly on the picture with drags, arrow keys, the eight handles and the rotation grip."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Select a clip on the canvas, then drag it into place. The handles and the grip do the same job as the numbers on the [Picture tab](/canvas/transform/), with the picture in front of you.

<AtAGlance
  keys={['← → ↑ ↓', '⇧ + arrow', '⌥-drag', '⇧-drag', 'Esc']}
  where="The preview canvas"
  tools="set_video"
/>

## Move

Drag inside a clip's box to move it. Every selected clip moves by the same amount and keeps its place relative to the others, including a selected clip that isn't at the playhead. Clips on locked tracks stay where they are.

The move [snaps](/canvas/canvas-snapping/) to the canvas and to other layers. Snapping tests the clip you grabbed, so the whole selection clicks into place together.

## Nudge

With the canvas focused, the arrow keys move the selected clips one canvas pixel. Hold <kbd>⇧</kbd> to move them ten. Clicking the canvas gives it focus.

Each press is one undo step, called Nudge. A nudge doesn't snap, and clips on locked tracks stay put.

With nothing selected, or only locked clips, the keys do their usual job: <kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd> step the playhead by a frame, <kbd>⇧←</kbd> and <kbd>⇧→</kbd> by ten, and <kbd>↑</kbd> and <kbd>↓</kbd> go to the previous and next edit point.

## Scale

Drag a corner or edge handle. The opposite handle stays pinned in place, and the clip moves as it scales to keep it there. This works on a rotated clip too.

What a handle changes depends on the clip:

| Clip | Corner handles | Edge handles |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Video, image, still, graphic, nest | Scale the whole picture and keep its shape. | The same. A clip like this has one scale, so an edge handle can't stretch it. |
| [Shape](/text-and-shapes/shape-settings/) | Resize the box and keep its proportions. Hold <kbd>⇧</kbd> to free them. | Change only the width or only the height. |
| [Text](/text-and-shapes/text-box/) | Scale the text. | Left and right set the wrap width, with the clip's centre staying still. Top and bottom scale the text. |

A drag scales between 1 % and 1000 %. A shape's box and a text clip's wrap width stay between 4 and 20,000.

A drag acts on the front-most selected clip only, even with several selected.

## Scale about the centre

Hold <kbd>⌥</kbd> while you scale to keep the clip's centre still instead of the opposite handle.

## Rotate

Drag the round grip above the top edge to turn the clip about its centre. A positive angle turns it clockwise. However far you drag, the angle stays between −180° and 180°, so the inspector never shows a wound-up value.

## Snap the angle

Hold <kbd>⇧</kbd> while you rotate to snap the angle to 15° steps.

## Cancel a drag

Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> during a canvas drag to put everything back as it was at the press, with no undo step. This covers move, scale, rotate, crop, line end and obscure region drags. Timeline drags have no such cancel.

<kbd>⇧</kbd> can stay down, but <kbd>Esc</kbd> doesn't cancel while <kbd>⌥</kbd> or <kbd>⌘</kbd> is held, so let go of those first.

## The pivot

Rotation, the Picture tab's **Scale** field and a <kbd>⌥</kbd> scale drag all pivot on the centre of the clip's uncropped picture. There's no separate anchor-point control. Because the pivot is the uncropped centre, cropping never moves it.

## One undo step per drag

Each canvas drag is one undo step, however many clips it moved, and a click that moves nothing adds no step. The steps are named Move, Scale, Rotate and Crop, so the Edit menu reads **Undo Move**, for example.

## Good to know

- With an action selected, these gestures change that action's end state rather than the clip. See [With an action selected](/canvas/the-canvas/#with-an-action-selected).
- In [crop mode](/canvas/crop/) the eight handles crop the clip instead of scaling it.

## Related

- [Position, scale, rotation and opacity](/canvas/transform/)
- [Canvas snapping](/canvas/canvas-snapping/)
- [Lines and arrows](/text-and-shapes/lines-and-arrows/)
- [Undo and saving](/getting-started/undo-and-saving/)

---
title: "Canvas snapping"
description: "Line a clip up with the canvas and other layers as you move it, and turn the pull off for one drag."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

While you move a clip on the canvas, its box pulls into line with the canvas and with the other layers, and a guide line shows what it lined up with.

<AtAGlance
  menu="View ▸ Snapping"
  keys={['N', '⌘-drag']}
  where="The Snap checkbox in the timeline bar"
/>

## What snaps

Only a move snaps. While you drag a clip, its box snaps to:

- the canvas's edges, its centre lines and its thirds
- the edges and centres of every other layer drawn at the playhead, including clips on locked tracks

Frame Job tests the clip's edges and its centre on each axis, and the smallest correction wins. The pull reaches 8 points on screen at any zoom, so it covers fewer canvas pixels the further you zoom in. A snap always lands on a whole canvas pixel.

A turned clip snaps by the bounds of its rotated box. With several clips selected, the clip you grabbed is the one tested, and the others in the drag aren't targets.

Scaling, rotating, cropping and arrow-key nudges don't snap. <kbd>⇧</kbd> while rotating [snaps the angle](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/#snap-the-angle) instead.

## Guide lines

A guide line is drawn across the whole canvas on each axis that snapped, so you can see what the clip lined up with. It's only there during the drag.

## Suspend for one drag

Hold <kbd>⌘</kbd> during a drag to stop snapping for as long as it's down. It works from the press or at any point during the drag, and snapping comes back when you let go of <kbd>⌘</kbd>.

## Turn snapping off

Press <kbd>N</kbd>, choose **View ▸ Snapping**, or use the **Snap** checkbox in the timeline bar. Snapping is on to begin with, and Frame Job remembers your choice. The canvas and the timeline share the one setting. See [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/).

## Related

- [Move, scale and rotate](/canvas/move-scale-rotate/)
- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
- [Safe areas](/canvas/safe-areas/)

---
title: "Safe areas"
description: "Show guide frames over the picture to keep titles and action clear of the canvas's edges."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Safe areas are two guide frames over the picture. Use them to keep titles and important action away from the edges, where a screen or a player's controls can cover them.

<AtAGlance
  menu="View ▸ Safe Areas"
  where="The Safe checkbox in the toolbar"
/>

## Safe area guides

Choose **View ▸ Safe Areas**, or tick **Safe** in the toolbar. Two centred frames appear, one at 90 % of the canvas's width and height and one at 80 %. On a 1920 × 1080 canvas that's 1728 × 972 and 1536 × 864.

The frames aren't labelled, and the inner one is drawn fainter. The menu item has a checkmark while they show.

The guides are off to begin with, and Frame Job remembers your choice between launches.

## Good to know

- The percentages are of the canvas, not the pane, so the frames zoom and pan with the picture.
- They take no clicks, so everything under them still works.
- They're guides only. They never appear in an export or a saved frame.

## Related

- [The canvas](/canvas/the-canvas/)
- [Canvas size](/projects/canvas-size/)
- [Canvas snapping](/canvas/canvas-snapping/)
